issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette: Samantha, a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and a Project Manager, has been grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening illness that she endured two years ago. The traumatic event has left indelible marks on her psyche, manifesting in various symptoms that have significantly impacted her daily life. The incident began as a routine medical check-up but quickly escalated when Samantha was diagnosed with a severe and unexpected illness. The hospital environment, filled with the scent of antiseptics and cold temperatures, became synonymous with fear and vulnerability. During her treatment, she endured multiple invasive procedures involving needles and intravenous drips, each one reinforcing the feeling that her body had been invaded and damaged beyond repair. In the months following her discharge from the hospital, Samantha found herself constantly trying to erase the memory of the event. She would distract herself with work projects or household chores, attempting to push the traumatic experience out of her mind. However, this effort was often futile as she would be suddenly overwhelmed by the intense emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory accompanying it. This disconnect made her feel that the memory was too extreme to believe it had actually happened to her. Samantha's fear extended beyond just the memories; she became hyper-vigilant, constantly monitoring her own thoughts for signs of going crazy. The mere sight of medical equipment, hospitals, ambulances, or even the prospect of a physical examination would send her into a panic. She avoided any reminders of the traumatic event, including places that smelled like antiseptics and cold environments reminiscent of the hospital. This avoidance behavior had significant consequences in both her personal life and work. As a Project Manager, Samantha found herself struggling to attend mandatory health screenings at her workplace, leading to missed opportunities for promotions and increased stress from potential health concerns going undetected. Her husband noticed that she became increasingly distant and irritable, avoiding family gatherings where medical topics might come up in conversation. Samantha's negative appraisals of the trauma have been deeply internalized. She believes that her life has been destroyed by this event and that she has failed in her most important role-whether it be as a wife or a professional. The physical vulnerability she feels is a constant reminder of the permanent damage her body has endured, leading to a pervasive sense of fragility and fear. Despite these challenges, Samantha's symptoms had gradually worsened over time, reaching a point where she could no longer function effectively in her daily life. The culmination was when she found herself unable to attend an important work conference due to her intense fears about being near medical personnel or feeling cold temperatures, which ultimately led to significant professional consequences. It was this breakdown that finally prompted Samantha to seek help. She is most afraid of reliving the traumatic experience and losing control over her emotions and thoughts. However, she also hopes for a way to reconcile the fragmented memories and intense feelings so that she can regain a sense of normalcy in her life and fulfill her roles both personally and professionally.
